one_liner: Parallel, full-format Matrix Market (.mtx) reader/writer; about 10x single-thread and 30x on 8 threads over IOStreams loaders.
what_it_does: Reads and writes Matrix Market files (coordinate and array, all fields and symmetries, matrix and vector objects) into triplet/doublet vectors, dense arrays, or directly into Eigen, GraphBLAS, CXSparse, Blaze and Armadillo types. The API is free functions such as read_matrix_market_triplet(std::istream&, nrows, ncols, rows, cols, vals) and write_matrix_market_csc(); you pass a std::istream/ostream plus your containers, and a read_options/write_options struct controls threads and chunk size. It replaces a library's own mmread/mmwrite rather than any standard API, and its Python binding is what scipy.io.mmread/mmwrite use from SciPy 1.12.
how_it_is_fast: Field conversion uses fast_float or C++17 std::from_chars for numbers and Dragonbox/Ryu or std::to_chars for writing, avoiding scanf/strtod/IOStreams, which also lock on the locale and get slower with threads. The main thread reads the stream in 2 MiB line-aligned chunks; a thread pool counts lines per chunk so each chunk's output offset (coordinate) or row/column start (array) is known, then parses chunks in parallel straight into presized output vectors. Bounded in-flight chunks give backpressure, and chunk buffers are reused to keep RSS down.
when_to_use: Loading multi-GB SuiteSparse or graph .mtx files into C++ where the existing loader (Eigen's loadMarket, hand-written scanf/IOStreams code) is the bottleneck

Coordinate files with real/integer/complex/pattern fields read into std::vector-like triplets or CSC/CSR; the example output shows about 500 MB/s on one thread and about 1.6 GB/s on 8 threads on an M1 Pro
Writing large sparse or dense results to .mtx, including CSC/CSR directly without a COO intermediate
Python on SciPy older than 1.12, or when you need vector files, longdouble or direct CSR/CSC writes, which scipy.io.mmread lacks (pip or conda fast_matrix_market)
Files SuiteSparse ships that partial loaders reject: array format, vector objects, skew-symmetric/hermitian, 64-bit indices
when_not_to_use: Small files where load time is already negligible; the gain only matters at hundreds of MB and up
Binary formats would be faster still: if you control both ends, a binary sparse format avoids text parsing altogether
Some paths fall back to sequential: bool value types, symmetric array files, and coordinate files read into dense handlers do not parallelize
Toolchains without float std::from_chars and with fast_float disabled fall back to strtod, which the author's parse-bench shows serializing on the locale lock
If you need an actively maintained dependency: last commit June 2024, PyPI wheels stop at CPython 3.12 (1.7.6, December 2023)

integration.form: header-only (CMake INTERFACE target; header-only only when the optional fast_float, Dragonbox and Ryu dependencies are disabled)
integration.dependencies: C++11 threads; optional and on by default: fast_float, Dragonbox, Ryu (vendored under dependencies/); bundled task_thread_pool header. Eigen/GraphBLAS/CXSparse/Blaze/Armadillo only for their bindings
integration.min_toolchain: C++17, CMake 3.14+; CI tests GCC 8 and 13, LLVM/Clang 8, MSVC and MinGW 13 (CMake probes for std::from_chars/std::to_chars support)
integration.platforms: any platform with C++17 and std::thread (CI: Linux, macOS, Windows; PyPI wheels for x86-64 and aarch64)
integration.thread_safety: Each call uses its own thread pool, default std::thread::hardware_concurrency() threads (read_options.num_threads, parallel_ok); concurrent calls on separate streams are not documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: a replacement for scipy.io.mmread/mmwrite (the same functions in SciPy 1.12+) and for library loaders, but C++ callers switch to its free-function API with a std::istream

gotchas: Open output streams in binary mode; text mode on Windows writes CRLF line endings that other loaders may reject

Symmetric files are expanded to general by default (generalize_symmetry=true); a diagonal entry gets an extra explicit zero (ExtraZeroElement) unless the app binding generalizes, so nnz can differ from what other loaders produce
Output vectors are resized from the header's nnz before parsing, so a corrupt or hostile header can force a very large allocation before any error is raised
Uses all hardware threads by default; set num_threads (C++) or parallelism (Python) inside already-parallel programs
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No sibling does the same job: the other sparse-and-solvers entries (merge-spmv, CSR5, AMGCL, Ginkgo) are kernels and solvers that need their input loaded first. Use this as their I/O front end when .mtx parsing dominates benchmark or pipeline start-up time.
verified_claims_summary: First-party Google Benchmark (benchmark/fmm_bench via run_benchmarks.sh, CMake Release, compiler not stated) on an 8-core Apple M1 Pro: coordinate reads 1578 MB/s on 8 threads vs 48.5 MB/s for a sequential IOStreams loader (about 32x; about 10x on one thread); coordinate writes 691 MB/s vs 60.9 MB/s (about 11x; 3.6x on one thread). The README's '>1 GB/s, about 25x' headline holds for reads and for array writes, not for coordinate writes.
status_note: Stale since June 2024 (C++ header version 1.7.7, PyPI 1.7.6) but feature-complete, BSD-2-Clause and shipped inside SciPy 1.12+, so it is safe to vendor; open issues are build and packaging requests, not bugs.
